Hi, friends! Happy Thursday!

You’ve seen The Wizard of Oz... the ruby slippers, the Yellow Brick Road, the flying monkeys… But you've also heard rumblings of some dark rumors, haven't you?

Well, behind all that glitter and Technicolor magic was a nightmare of toxic makeup, real fires, starvation diets, terror in Munchkinland and a studio system that nearly killed a teenage Judy Garland.

In today’s episode of Dark History, let's follow the (bloodsoaked?) yellow brick road backstage to uncover the shocking truth behind one of Hollywood’s most iconic movies.

From the Tin Man’s near-death experience to the Witch catching fire on set (literally), to asbestos snow and all sorts of horrible abuse — this is the wicked story of The Wizard of Oz that MGM never wanted you to hear.

When I was little (I think it was probably in 1989 so I would have been about five) my parents tape recorded The Wizard of Oz for us. We used to watch it so often I think we nearly wore out the VHS 😂

Interestingly, I did not see the very end of the film for many years, because just at the part where the Scarecrow says, "What have you learned, Dorothy?" and she replied, "Well, I, I..." the tape ran out. I have only seen the very end a handful of times. 

Prior to the start of the actual film for that broadcast, they had a number of entertainment professionals talking about it. Two examples I remember well are Marlee Matlin and Jim Henson. Matlin spoke about how watching the film made her feel that as a little girl she could have dreams just like Dorothy's, and even growing up and now being a woman she was still that little girl inside. Henson said that it was the very first film he had ever seen, and it was still his favourite. He said he felt that this picture was a wonderful thing for the whole fantasy world, and allowed for the creation of other fantasy worlds. (In case anybody doesn't realize the significance of this comment: Jim Henson created The Muppets, Sesame Street, and Fraggle Rock.)

Angela Lansbury also mentioned a few things about the film and its creation. She said that Jack Haley couldn't sit down in his costume; he had to lean against an oversized ironing board to rest. Ray Bolger's face would bleed at the end of the day because the makeup he wore as the Scarecrow made his skin incredibly raw. Bert Lahr's lion costume was according to him, "like walking around inside a wet mattress". (I later read a quote from Bert Lahr in which he said that The Wizard of Oz kind of ruined his career, because after that he was sort of typecast as a lion, and there just weren't many parts for lions.)
